chunk_findings.detail: The change implements the refusal path but not the promised explicit override path. `unknown_needs()` is called unconditionally in both add paths and in `update`; nothing in the changed code threads or honors an override flag. For example, the documented escape hatch from the acceptance criteria (`ddflow task add Tx --title t --needs NOPE-123 --force`, or the equivalent explicit flag) still returns `O.failed` because line 78/254 calls `IT.unknown_needs(...)` before any bypass, and `_edit.py:195` does the same for `--needs`/`--add-needs`. Thus the behavior is “always refuse,” not “refuse unless an explicit flag is given,” which fails the stated requirement that override be possible only with an explicit flag.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:78 (and :254; also ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:195)

chunk_findings.detail: These refusal tests assert only that the CLI exits non-zero and echoes the bad id; they do not assert that the queue was left unchanged. For example, if `task add T --title t --needs NO-SUCH-ID` creates task `T`, then prints an error and returns 1, lines 18-20 pass even though the command did not “refuse” in the intended sense. The same weakness applies to `update T --add-needs GHOST` and `update T --needs A,GHOST`: an implementation that mutates dependencies before validation can leave `GHOST` recorded or otherwise corrupt the item and still pass because only exit status/message are checked.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:16

chunk_findings.detail: `test_task_add_names_the_nearest_real_id` does not actually verify that the nearest real id is named. With tasks `A` and `B` present, it only asserts that the output contains the substring `"Did you mean"`. A CLI that prints `"Did you mean B?"` or `"Did you mean ?"` for `--needs Aa` would pass this test, even though the nearest id is `A` and the promised behavior is to name the nearest real id.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:23

chunk_findings.detail: `_adjust_list(it, edit, fields, "needs")` merges the requested `--add-needs` value with the item’s existing needs into `fields["needs"]`, and `IT.unknown_needs` is then called on that merged list. An item created before this fix may already contain an unknown need (the old code accepted it), so a valid command such as `ddflow task update T --add-needs REAL` will fail with `"no such id 'NOPE'"`, where `NOPE` is the pre-existing invalid dependency, not an ID supplied by this update. The check should validate only the newly supplied `--needs`/`--add-needs` arguments, not the final merged list.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:193-194

chunk_findings.detail: The refusal tests only assert a nonzero exit code and that the unknown id appears in output; none verifies the state was actually refused. For example, an implementation of `task add T --needs NO-SUCH-ID` that prints `NO-SUCH-ID`, returns 1, but still creates `T` would pass `test_task_add_refuses_an_unknown_need`, so the regression test does not prove the dependent task was not filed and the original bug can remain in a weaker form.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:19

A `--needs` replacement path that validates or merges the item's current needs rather than only the ids supplied by the update would still refuse the valid command `ddflow task update T --needs A` on old items containing `OLD-GHOST`, and the suite would not catch it.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_add_needs_valid_id_is_not_refused_on_a_pre_existing_unknown_need

chunk_findings.detail: The two update refusal tests were changed from `GHOST` to `Aa`. `Aa` has a nearest existing id (`A`), so both tests now exercise only the suggestion branch (`Did you mean 'A'`). An update implementation that still silently accepts a truly nonexistent id when no suggestion exists—for example `ddflow task update T --add-needs GHOST` returns 0 and stores `GHOST`—would pass these tests. That is exactly the original bug class, so the update paths lose regression coverage for the no-near-match case.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_update_add_needs_refuses_an_unknown_need and test_update_needs_refuses_an_unknown_need

chunk_findings.detail: The change implements the refusal path but not the promised explicit override path. `unknown_needs()` is called unconditionally in both add paths and in `update`; nothing in the changed code threads or honors an override flag. For example, the documented escape hatch from the acceptance criteria (`ddflow task add Tx --title t --needs NOPE-123 --force`, or the equivalent explicit flag) still returns `O.failed` because line 78/254 calls `IT.unknown_needs(...)` before any bypass, and `_edit.py:195` does the same for `--needs`/`--add-needs`. Thus the behavior is “always refuse,” not “refuse unless an explicit flag is given,” which fails the stated requirement that override be possible only with an explicit flag.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_add.py:78 (and :254; also ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:195)

chunk_findings.detail: These refusal tests assert only that the CLI exits non-zero and echoes the bad id; they do not assert that the queue was left unchanged. For example, if `task add T --title t --needs NO-SUCH-ID` creates task `T`, then prints an error and returns 1, lines 18-20 pass even though the command did not “refuse” in the intended sense. The same weakness applies to `update T --add-needs GHOST` and `update T --needs A,GHOST`: an implementation that mutates dependencies before validation can leave `GHOST` recorded or otherwise corrupt the item and still pass because only exit status/message are checked.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:16

chunk_findings.detail: `test_task_add_names_the_nearest_real_id` does not actually verify that the nearest real id is named. With tasks `A` and `B` present, it only asserts that the output contains the substring `"Did you mean"`. A CLI that prints `"Did you mean B?"` or `"Did you mean ?"` for `--needs Aa` would pass this test, even though the nearest id is `A` and the promised behavior is to name the nearest real id.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:23

chunk_findings.detail: `_adjust_list(it, edit, fields, "needs")` merges the requested `--add-needs` value with the item’s existing needs into `fields["needs"]`, and `IT.unknown_needs` is then called on that merged list. An item created before this fix may already contain an unknown need (the old code accepted it), so a valid command such as `ddflow task update T --add-needs REAL` will fail with `"no such id 'NOPE'"`, where `NOPE` is the pre-existing invalid dependency, not an ID supplied by this update. The check should validate only the newly supplied `--needs`/`--add-needs` arguments, not the final merged list.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/items/_edit.py:193-194

chunk_findings.detail: The refusal tests only assert a nonzero exit code and that the unknown id appears in output; none verifies the state was actually refused. For example, an implementation of `task add T --needs NO-SUCH-ID` that prints `NO-SUCH-ID`, returns 1, but still creates `T` would pass `test_task_add_refuses_an_unknown_need`, so the regression test does not prove the dependent task was not filed and the original bug can remain in a weaker form.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:19

chunk_findings.detail: `test_task_add_names_the_nearest_real_id` only checks the string `"Did you mean"`, not the suggested id. With the input `--needs Aa`, an implementation that suggests the wrong real id (`Did you mean B?`) would still pass, even though the intent explicitly requires naming the nearest real id.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:27

chunk_findings.detail: This test still only checks that the command exits non-zero and prints the nearest-id hint; it does not check that the task was not filed. Given `task add T2 --title t2 --needs Aa`, an implementation that creates `T2`, then validates the need, prints `Did you mean 'A'`, and exits 1 would pass this test while still filing a task with an unknown dependency. The refusal test for `NO-SUCH-ID` now guards against that, but the near-match path remains unguarded.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_task_add_names_the_nearest_real_id

chunk_findings.detail: The acceptance criterion covers override behavior for both `update --needs` and `update --add-needs`, but the new override test exercises only `update T --needs A,NOPE --allow-unknown-needs`. If the override flag is threaded only through the `--needs` code path (or only through `task add`), then `update T --add-needs NOPE --allow-unknown-needs` could still be refused, yet the test suite would pass because no test invokes that command.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_update_allow_unknown_needs_overrides_the_refusal

chunk_findings.detail: Both update refusal tests assert only a nonzero exit, the unknown id in output, and unchanged needs. After `_two(repo)` creates A and B, an update implementation that returns 1 and prints `GHOST` for `update T --add-needs GHOST` or `update T --needs A,GHOST` but never prints `"Did you mean 'A'"` still passes both tests. The B4d23497469 acceptance calls for update `--needs`/`--add-needs` to name the nearest real id, so the regression suite would accept a fix that only adds the hint to `task add`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_update_add_needs_refuses_an_unknown_need, test_update_needs_refuses_an_unknown_need

chunk_findings.detail: No test exercises `update T --add-needs GHOST --allow-unknown-needs`. The update override test uses `--needs A,NOPE`, but `--add-needs` goes through a different merge/validation path in `_edit.py`. An implementation that honors the explicit override for `task add` and `update --needs` but still refuses `update --add-needs GHOST` passes every test in this file, leaving a required update path unprotected.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_update_allow_unknown_needs_overrides_the_refusal

chunk_findings.detail: Both update near-match refusal tests create task `T` with `--needs A` and then supply the typo `Aa`, whose nearest real id is also `A`. Because `A` is already in `T.needs`, the assertion `_items(repo)["T"].needs == ["A"]` cannot distinguish a true refusal from an implementation that auto-corrects `Aa` to `A`, mutates the task, prints `Did you mean 'A'`, and exits 1. For example, if the code treated an unknown near-match as “did you mean X? I’ll use X” and applied it, these tests would still pass (after deduplication) even though the acceptance criterion requires the command to refuse and leave the task unchanged. To prove refusal, the near-match case should target a real id that is not already a need, e.g. `update T --add-needs Ba` when `T` only needs `A`; the expected `needs` would stay `["A"]` and the hint should name `B`, so an auto-correction would be caught as `["A", "B"]`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_update_add_needs_names_the_nearest_real_id, tests/test_task_add_unknown_need.py:test_update_needs_names_the_nearest_real_id

chunk_findings.detail: The test never verifies that the setup actually created the pre-existing unknown need before the update. `task add T --title t --needs OLD-GHOST --allow-unknown-needs` is only checked for exit code 0, and the final assertion is `_items(repo)["T"].needs == ["A"]` after `update T --needs A`. If an implementation’s add/override path returns 0 but silently does not persist `OLD-GHOST`, there is no pre-existing unknown need, the valid update succeeds, and this test still passes—so the refusal-on-pre-existing-unknown-need path it is meant to guard can remain uncovered.
